near_miss.lead: Wife of X, daughter of Y: kona/dóttir beside γυνή/θυγάτηρ
near_miss.why_not: Both kinship nouns are cognate and identify a woman by husband and father, but these are literal biographical identifications. The order differs and there is no distinctive poetic or juridical expression beyond normal kinship syntax.

near_miss.lead: Hearing words: heyrðir orð / uerba audire
near_miss.why_not: The Norse political accusations, Lucretian explanation of indistinct hearing, and Plautine response have ordinary verb–object syntax. A search of all local LASLA conllup files also found the combination at Cato Orationum fragment 111.5 and Catullus 61.97–98 and 84.8–9; Celtic searches found ordinary hearing-of-words narrative uses. Shared lexical material does not establish a distinctive inherited phrase.

near_miss.lead: Cattle and killing: kýr ... til bana / gām haṃsi
near_miss.why_not: Cattle are victims in both passages, but the Norse construction is passive wounding with a result phrase, whereas the Vedic charm has active killing with direct objects and retaliatory piercing. The cow/horse/man series is absent in Norse. A literal common event does not establish inherited wording.

anchors: ang:Grein I A Za R I A S l.10871
near_miss.lead: Frost and snow: Reód/sneachta, frost/sníor, forst/sniw, nix/pruina
near_miss.why_not: The cognate weather nouns are real, but the contexts differ: exposure lament, cosmic winter, Christian praise, divine immunity to weather, and meteorological explanation. Celtic corpus searches found the pair in annalistic reports (Ulster U1111.1 and U1115.1, among others), and LASLA confirms both Lucretian examples. Old English Grein text confirms the Christian address. These are natural weather lists with varying syntax and order; the evidence does not discriminate inherited phraseology from independent enumeration or Christian textual transmission.

near_miss.lead: Night/day as completeness: nótt ok dag, νύκτες/ἡμέραι, divā naktaṃ
near_miss.why_not: The Norse surveillance passage and Vedic protective wakefulness can be compared, but only night supplies secure common lexical material; Greek turns nights into days in a story of evading an oracle. Searches of LASLA found night/day pairs widely in comedy, philosophy, and agriculture, including Cato 109.1 and 150.1. This universally available temporal merism lacks a distinctive shared inherited construction here.

near_miss.lead: Water handling: jóst ... vatni / ἀφυσσάμεθ᾽ ὕδωρ
near_miss.why_not: The verb and water noun are plausibly cognate, but Norse refers to sprinkling a person (personal object plus instrumental dative water), while Homer describes drawing a ship’s water supply (water as direct object). Searching Menota XML as text found repeated infant water-sprinkling/name-giving uses in AM-35-fol, Laxdaela saga, and Wolf-Aug-9-10-4to. These support the Norse ritual sense without supplying its counterpart in the Greek anchors. No shared ritual wording demonstrated.

near_miss.lead: Milking cows: bhleaghan na mbó / mjólka kýr
near_miss.why_not: Irish bhleaghan is the lenited verbal noun of bligh with genitive plural mbó; Norse has an infinitive with accusative plural kýr. Both roots agree, but the collocation is the ordinary literal activity. Searching Celtic units found further daily milking contexts in G201001 #1/1/#14 and G201009 #1/18. Feeding Suibhne and a housewife’s dairy work share no distinctive figurative, metrical, or ritual constraint.

Irish athair and máthair are nominative singular list members in a report of family deaths; Latin matribus/patribus occur in plague deaths, while Vedic pitaraṃ/mātaraṃ are objects in a protective prohibition. Norse genealogy links successive generations rather than coordinating parents of one child. A family list, plague scene, and protection from a child do not share a specific inherited construction beyond elementary kinship vocabulary.

The Norse calendar calculation and the Vedic wish to see/live a hundred autumns share numerical and temporal vocabulary, but Norse counts days in a calendar year rather than human lifespan. The Vedic repeated blessing has no Norse syntactic or contextual counterpart.

The Norse three winters and three summers expresses a stay and accumulated earnings; the Sanskrit stay is prolonged ascetic residence. Seasonal reckoning is ordinary and there is no matching numeral or marked formula in the two anchors.

near_miss.lead: Seeing light: edrỳch ... goleu versus darśata/rocanas and dadṛśur/rukma
near_miss.why_not: Welsh edrych is a verbal noun governed by an instruction to look at light; the eyes are then opened and closed. The Sanskrit contexts concern visible or shining ornament, a gold-backed bow, and spectators. These do not reproduce the Welsh construction or context. Lexical root overlap includes derivative substitutions that are not phraseological evidence.

The Greek aftermath of massacre includes infertility of earth, women, and flocks; Sanskrit threatens destruction of the Kauravas together with sons, livestock, and relatives. This is a tempting total-destruction theme, but the enumerated categories and predication differ and a matching cognate collocation is not established. The Norse pivot concerns anticipated wealth, not fertility or a curse.

Irish duille participates in a comparison between the psalter and a yew’s leaves, whereas Latin folia are literal leaves under a cake. The Irish wordplay has no Latin counterpart; brightness vocabulary is attached to different things. The plant noun alone cannot support inherited phraseology.
